newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: PLO wants U.N. mission sent to occupied territories.
newsitem.headline: PLO wants U.N. mission sent to occupied territories.

text.p: Palestinian leader Farouk Kaddoumi called on the Security Council on Friday to demand that Israel permanently close a tunnel in Jerusalem that has sparked three days of violence and to send a fact-finding mission to examine the deteriorating situation.

More than 65 people have been killed and hundreds wounded in the Israeli-occupied territories since Israel this week opened a new entrance to an archaeological tunnel near Jerusalem's al-Aqsa mosque, Islam's third-holiest shrine.

Kaddoumi, who heads the Palestine Liberation Organisation's political department, said what had happened resulted from "an accumulation of simmering tensions" for which Israel alone bore full responsibility.

He cited a long list of actions by Israel's recently elected right-wing government led by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, including the resumption of settlement activities, confiscation of Arab land, destruction of a community centre in East Jerusalem, failure to withdraw from the West Bank town of Hebron and sealing of the occupied territories.

If Israel's "brutal measures" continued, the Middle East peace process would be "in mortal peril," Kadoumi said. "These require denunciation from this council and a demand that Israel put an end to its provocative acts and close the tunnel in order to defuse the escalating tensions," he said.

"We recommend that this council dispatch a fact-finding mission and call for peace in the occupied territories and examine in full detail the situation there." The council should then take appropriate measures, he added.

Israeli Foreign Minister David Levy, who spoke next, attacked what he called an "orchestrated attempt to place blame on Israel and to portray her as the sole responsible party for the bitter harvest of blood" in which scores of Palestinians and Israelis had lost their lives.

"I come to refute in their entirety the distortions of facts which are being spread here regarding the dramatic effects of the last days and which have cast such a dark cloud over the entire peace process," Levy said.

Whatever claims were made against Israel, they in no way justified the "incitement to violence and the use of live weapons," he said. "The atmosphere of escalation and the threats and the calls for armed struggle will not move us from the fundamental principles which guide our policy: the pursuit of peace while ensuring national and personal security for our citizens."
The Jerusalem tunnel had no religious significance and the issue was being manipulated, Levy said, adding that Israel safeguarded the freedom of worship of all faiths.
The debate was marked by the participation of a number of foreign ministers in New York for the U.N. General Assembly.
Egyptian Foreign Minister Amre Moussa called Israel's policy on the peace process "shameful stalling" and called on it to implement agreements already made with the Palestinians.

"The alternative to peace is something the international community cannot bear ... Israel must relinquish this negative policy ... The Security Council must send a strong, unambiguous message to the Israeli government," he said.

British Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind called for a moratorium on opening the tunnel, which Israel announced on Friday had been temporarily closed. Like many other speakers, he also called for a meeting between Netanyahu and Palestinian President Yasser Arafat.
Rifkind also backed a proposal by Jordan's King Hussein for an international commission to "work out ways of dealing with the sensitive questions that arise in Jerusalem on archaeological matters."
Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov criticised Israel for stalling on the Middle East peace process and said the latest crisis was a "direct result of reckless activity."
"Russia urges strongly all the interested parties to show maxmimum restraint and to avoid action that would worsen the situation," he added.

French Foreign Minister Herve de Charette also criticised Israel and called for closing of the controversial tunnel. The peace process was "in danger of seeing its death-knell if the international community does not act quickly and firmly," he said.
